title: Ottoman Egypt
subtitle: 1517–1798 · The Eyalet, the Return of the Mamluks, and the Eve of the Modern

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: An Ottoman province where the pashas faded and the Mamluk households returned — to Ali Bey's brief independence and the duumvirate the French destroyed

entries.label: Selim I conquers Egypt
entries.hint: Selim I's army, with its field artillery and arquebusiers, destroyed the Mamluk cavalry at Marj Dabiq in 1516 and again at al-Raydaniyya outside Cairo in January 1517. The last Mamluk sultan, Tuman Bay, was caught after weeks of street fighting and hanged at the Bab Zuwayla. Egypt, an independent sultanate for two and a half centuries, became a province of the Ottoman empire, and Selim took the guardianship of the Holy Cities and, in later tradition, the caliphal title.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas, Bada'i' al-zuhur (an eyewitness). Michael Winter, Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule 1517–1798 (1992) pp.7–13; Benjamin Lellouch, Les Ottomans en Égypte: historiens et conquérants au XVIe siècle (2006).

entries.label: Khayr Bey and the first governors
entries.hint: Selim left Egypt under Khayr Bey, the Mamluk governor of Aleppo whose defection had helped win Marj Dabiq, as the first Ottoman viceroy. Khayr Bey kept much of the Mamluk apparatus and many Mamluk officers in place while an Ottoman garrison and Ottoman fiscal officials were installed alongside them. The compromise — Ottoman sovereignty over a still-partly-Mamluk administration — set the pattern for the whole period.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas; Winter, Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule (1992) pp.14–17; P.M. Holt, Egypt and the Fertile Crescent 1516–1922 (1966) pp.45–50.

entries.label: The Qanunname and the ordered eyalet
entries.hint: After the governor Ahmad Pasha revolted and briefly declared himself an independent sultan, the grand vizier Ibrahim Pasha came in person and issued the Qanunname-i Misir — a detailed code fixing the governor's powers, the seven military corps and their pay, the fiscal districts and the annual tribute (irsaliyye) owed to Istanbul, and the provisioning of Mecca and Medina. It was the constitution of Ottoman Egypt, cited as authoritative down to Bonaparte.
entries.note: Ömer Lütfi Barkan, XV ve XVI Asırlarda Osmanlı İmparatorluğunda Ziraî Ekonominin Hukukî ve Malî Esasları (1943) prints the qanunname. Stanford Shaw, The Financial and Administrative Organization and Development of Ottoman Egypt (1962).

entries.label: The pashas fade
entries.hint: Ottoman governors were rotated through Egypt every year or two, and by the seventeenth century most could not control the entrenched military corps or the reviving Mamluk beys. The local soldiery took to deposing an unsatisfactory pasha by acclamation — 'casting him out' — and appointing an acting governor until Istanbul sent another. Real authority drained from the Citadel to the barracks and the great households.
entries.note: Winter, Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule (1992) pp.20–34; Jane Hathaway, The Politics of Households in Ottoman Egypt: The Rise of the Qazdağlıs (1997) pp.7–16.

entries.label: The Mamluk households return
entries.hint: The Mamluk system quietly reconstituted itself under Ottoman rule. Grandees — the beys who held the twenty-four sanjak commands — built up households (bayts) of imported Caucasian slave-soldiers trained and freed as before, competing for the key offices of shaykh al-balad (senior bey) and amir al-hajj (commander of the pilgrimage caravan). Two rival blocs, the Faqari and the Qasimi, structured the politics of the century.
entries.note: Hathaway, The Politics of Households in Ottoman Egypt (1997); P.M. Holt, 'The Beylicate in Ottoman Egypt during the Seventeenth Century', BSOAS 24 (1961).

entries.label: Ridwan Bey al-Faqari
entries.hint: Ridwan Bey held the office of amir al-hajj almost continuously for a quarter of a century, the most powerful figure in Egypt while a succession of pashas came and went. His Faqari household and the rival Qasimi bloc under Ali Bey dominated the middle of the century, and his ascendancy established the model that would run to 1798: a single great bey, backed by his own household troops, overshadowing the Ottoman governor.
entries.note: P.M. Holt, 'The Career of Küçük Muhammad (1676–94)', BSOAS 26 (1963) and 'The Pattern of Egyptian Political History from 1517 to 1798', in Holt (ed.), Political and Social Change in Modern Egypt (1968).

entries.label: The Qazdughli ascendancy
entries.hint: A household founded within the Janissary corps by an officer called Qazdughli grew, over two generations, to dominate both the corps and the beylicate, absorbing or destroying its rivals. In the 1740s and 1750s Ibrahim Kahya and Ridwan Kahya ran Egypt as a 'dual amirate'. When Ibrahim died his mamluks fought for the succession, and out of that contest rose Ali Bey al-Kabir.
entries.note: Jane Hathaway, The Politics of Households in Ottoman Egypt: The Rise of the Qazdağlıs (1997). Daniel Crecelius, The Roots of Modern Egypt (1981) pp.31–44.

entries.label: Ali Bey al-Kabir
entries.hint: Ali Bey, a Qazdughli mamluk of Georgian origin, eliminated his rivals, made himself shaykh al-balad, and by 1768 was expelling Ottoman governors, withholding the tribute, and striking coins in his own name — the first ruler to detach Egypt from Istanbul since 1517. He annexed the Hijaz and, in 1770–71, sent his army under Abu al-Dhahab to take Damascus in league with the Galilee shaykh Zahir al-Umar and, at a distance, with Russia, then at war with the Ottomans.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti, 'Aja'ib al-athar. Daniel Crecelius, The Roots of Modern Egypt: A Study of the Regimes of 'Ali Bey al-Kabir and Muhammad Bey Abu al-Dhahab, 1760–1775 (1981).

entries.label: Abu al-Dhahab's betrayal
entries.hint: Muhammad Bey Abu al-Dhahab, Ali Bey's chief lieutenant and freedman, abruptly abandoned the Syrian campaign in 1772, marched back on Cairo, and drove his master out. Ali Bey fled to Zahir al-Umar, returned in 1773 with a Russian squadron's help, was beaten at al-Salihiyya, captured, and died of his wounds. Abu al-Dhahab then ruled as shaykh al-balad, made peace with Istanbul, invaded Syria on the sultan's behalf, and died before Acre in 1775.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti, 'Aja'ib al-athar; Crecelius, The Roots of Modern Egypt (1981).

entries.label: Ibrahim Bey and Murad Bey
entries.hint: For the last quarter-century of Ottoman Egypt two of Abu al-Dhahab's freedmen, Ibrahim Bey the administrator and Murad Bey the soldier, ruled jointly — feuding, splitting the country between them, and squeezing it with new taxes and confiscations. An Ottoman expedition under Hasan Pasha drove them to Upper Egypt in 1786, but they were back within two years. Their army, still built around lance and sabre, was destroyed by Bonaparte's infantry squares at Imbaba in 1798.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti, 'Aja'ib al-athar; P.M. Holt, Egypt and the Fertile Crescent (1966) pp.85–100. The 1786 expedition: Stanford Shaw, Between Old and New: The Ottoman Empire under Sultan Selim III (1971).

entries.label: The French invasion
entries.hint: Bonaparte landed near Alexandria on 1 July 1798, beat the Mamluk cavalry at Imbaba across the Nile from Cairo on 21 July, and occupied the country for the French Directory, bringing 150-odd scholars and scientists whose survey became the Description de l'Égypte. Nelson destroyed the French fleet at Aboukir on 1 August, stranding the army; a Cairo uprising in October was put down with a bombardment of al-Azhar; and after Bonaparte slipped away, the occupation collapsed under a British and Ottoman assault in 1801.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti, three accounts of the French occupation (translated Moreh, Napoleon in Egypt, 1993). Henry Laurens, L'expédition d'Égypte 1798–1801 (1989); Juan Cole, Napoleon's Egypt (2007).

entries.label: The military corps as a power
entries.hint: Seven Ottoman regiments garrisoned Egypt, the most important the Janissaries (Mustahfizan) and the Azaban. Beyond soldiering they controlled lucrative revenues — the customs of the ports, the mints, market and protection dues — recruited local men and merchants into their ranks, and repeatedly deposed pashas and fought the beys. Over the eighteenth century the leading households and the corps effectively merged, and the corps as an independent force faded into the Mamluk world.
entries.note: Jane Hathaway, The Politics of Households in Ottoman Egypt (1997) pp.17–51; André Raymond, 'Soldiers in Trade: The Case of Ottoman Cairo', British Journal of Middle Eastern Studies 18 (1991).

entries.label: The Coptic patriarch and the archons
entries.hint: The Coptic patriarch, resident in Cairo, remained the head of the Christian community, a shrinking minority now but with a rising lay elite: the archons (arakhina), Coptic scribes, accountants and financiers indispensable to the tax administration and the Mamluk households. By the late eighteenth century Ibrahim al-Jawhari, a Copt, was in effect the chief financial officer of the whole regime, and his family endowed churches and monasteries on a scale not seen for centuries.
entries.note: Magdi Guirguis & Nelly van Doorn-Harder, The Emergence of the Modern Coptic Papacy (2011); Magdi Guirguis, An Armenian Artist in Ottoman Egypt: Yuhanna al-Armani and His Coptic Icons (2008). On the Jawharis: al-Jabarti.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Ottoman conquest, the revolts of pashas and soldiers, the Faqari–Qasimi wars, Ali Bey's Syrian campaign, and the French landing

entries.label: Marj Dabiq and al-Raydaniyya
entries.hint: The Mamluk state, still fighting on horseback with lance and bow and distrustful of the firearm, met an Ottoman army that used massed field guns and janissary muskets from behind a wagon-fort. At Marj Dabiq north of Aleppo in August 1516 the Mamluk sultan Qansuh al-Ghawri was killed and his army broken; at al-Raydaniyya outside Cairo in January 1517 the new sultan Tuman Bay's guns were outmanoeuvred. After days of street fighting he was betrayed, captured and hanged at the Bab Zuwayla.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas, Bada'i' al-zuhur (eyewitness). Robert Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986); David Ayalon, Gunpowder and Firearms in the Mamluk Kingdom (1956).

entries.label: Ahmad Pasha the Traitor
entries.hint: Ahmad Pasha, sent as governor after being passed over for grand vizier, seized the Citadel, minted coins, had the Friday sermon read in his own name, and proclaimed himself an independent sultan of Egypt — barely seven years into Ottoman rule. Loyal officers killed him in his bath within months. The revolt prompted Istanbul to send the grand vizier Ibrahim Pasha to reorganise the province the following year.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas; the Ottoman chronicles. Winter, Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule (1992) pp.17–19; Seyyid Muradi and others.

entries.label: The mutinies of the corps
entries.hint: The Ottoman regiments of Egypt rose again and again — over arrears of pay, debased coin, or a commander's death. In 1586 and 1589 the cavalry corps mutinied over pay; a general revolt in 1609 was crushed by Kara Mehmed Pasha in a campaign remembered as the 'second Ottoman conquest of Egypt'; and in 1711 a religious dispute set off nine months of fighting between the corps and the beys that wrecked quarters of Cairo. Between the mutinies the soldiers routinely deposed governors they disliked.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti and the earlier Ottoman-Egyptian chronicles (al-Damurdashi, al-Ishaqi). Winter, Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule (1992) pp.34–41; Hathaway, The Politics of Households (1997).

entries.label: The Faqari–Qasimi wars
entries.hint: Egypt's politics for nearly a century were structured by the feud between two Mamluk factional blocs, the Faqari (with white banners and the pomegranate emblem) and the Qasimi (red banners, disc emblem), which reached down into the villages and the guilds. Leaders were murdered at truce meetings; whole households were driven into exile or killed, the Faqari nearly annihilated in 1730. Neither the pasha nor the corps could stop it; the Qazdughli household finally absorbed the survivors of both.
entries.note: P.M. Holt, 'The Beylicate in Ottoman Egypt' (1961); Hathaway, The Politics of Households (1997) and A Tale of Two Factions: Myth, Memory, and Identity in Ottoman Egypt and Yemen (2003).

entries.label: Ali Bey's Syrian campaign
entries.hint: Ali Bey sent an Egyptian army north under Abu al-Dhahab and Isma'il Bey. It took Gaza and Jaffa, joined the Galilee shaykh Zahir al-Umar, beat the Ottoman governor of Damascus in the field, and entered the city in June 1771 — for a few days the Mamluks held both Cairo and Damascus. Then Abu al-Dhahab suddenly withdrew the whole army to Egypt, on a secret understanding with the Ottomans, and the campaign that had made Ali Bey a regional power collapsed.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti; the Ottoman and Damascene chronicles. Crecelius, The Roots of Modern Egypt (1981) pp.71–98; Thomas Philipp, Acre: The Rise and Fall of a Palestinian City 1730–1831 (2001).

entries.label: The war of Ali Bey and Abu al-Dhahab
entries.hint: Driven from Cairo, Ali Bey took refuge with Zahir al-Umar at Acre, where a Russian naval squadron operating against the Ottomans in the eastern Mediterranean shelled Ottoman ports on his behalf and Beirut was briefly taken. In April 1773 he marched back toward Egypt, was ambushed and defeated by Abu al-Dhahab's forces at al-Salihiyya, wounded and captured, and died a week later in his rival's custody.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti; Crecelius, The Roots of Modern Egypt (1981) pp.99–120. The Russian dimension: A.I. Bagis and the Chesme-era literature.

entries.label: The expedition of Hasan Pasha
entries.hint: In 1786 the Ottoman grand admiral Cezayirli Gazi Hasan Pasha landed with a fleet and army to break the beys and restore the tribute. He beat Murad Bey at al-Rahmaniyya, occupied Cairo, drove Ibrahim and Murad into Upper Egypt, cut taxes, and installed a compliant regime under Isma'il Bey. But when war with Russia broke out in 1787 he was recalled; within a year Ibrahim and Murad had returned, and the last Ottoman attempt to rule Egypt directly before Muhammad Ali was over.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti; Stanford Shaw, Between Old and New: The Ottoman Empire under Sultan Selim III (1971) pp.242–52; Daniel Crecelius (ed.), Eighteenth Century Egypt: The Arabic Manuscript Sources (1990).

entries.label: The Pyramids, Aboukir and the Cairo revolt
entries.hint: Bonaparte's infantry in squares broke Murad Bey's charging cavalry at Imbaba, opposite Cairo, on 21 July 1798 — the 'Battle of the Pyramids'. Ten days later Nelson annihilated the French fleet at anchor at Aboukir, trapping the army in Egypt. In October the population of Cairo rose against the occupiers, the fighting centring on al-Azhar; French artillery bombarded the mosque quarter, and the rising was crushed with mass executions. The occupation held on, isolated, until 1801.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti, Muddat al-faransis bi-misr and 'Aja'ib al-athar. Henry Laurens, L'expédition d'Égypte (1989); Juan Cole, Napoleon's Egypt (2007).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The eyalet, the qanunname, the seven military corps, and the iltizam tax-farm that put the countryside in private hands

entries.label: The eyalet and its offices
entries.hint: Egypt was governed on the standard Ottoman provincial template: a viceroy (pasha) with the rank of vizier, a council (divan), a chief Hanafi judge sent from Istanbul with a web of deputy qadis, a finance office keeping an annual budget, the seven military corps, and the obligation to remit a fixed tribute to the imperial treasury each year. The template stayed formally in place for 280 years even as the substance of power moved elsewhere.
entries.note: Stanford Shaw, The Financial and Administrative Organization and Development of Ottoman Egypt 1517–1798 (1962) and the translated Ottoman Egypt in the Age of the French Revolution (1964). Winter, Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule (1992).

entries.label: The iltizam tax-farm and the village
entries.hint: Direct state collection gave way to tax-farming: a multazim bought the right to collect a village's dues for a fixed payment plus recognised fees, kept the surplus, and held the farm for life and increasingly by inheritance. By the eighteenth century the beys, the ulama and Coptic financiers held most of the farms of Egypt, collecting through the village shaykh and the corvée, while the peasant's burden grew, the Bedouin took over whole districts, and villages emptied under the pressure.
entries.note: Kenneth Cuno, The Pasha's Peasants: Land, Society, and Economy in Lower Egypt 1740–1858 (1992); Stanford Shaw, The Financial and Administrative Organization... (1962). The Hawwara of Upper Egypt: al-Jabarti.

entries.label: Feeding Istanbul and the Holy Cities
entries.hint: Egypt owed the empire more than the cash tribute. It sent an annual shipment of grain and money for the poor of Mecca and Medina, outfitted and paid for the escort of the pilgrimage caravan, and its workshops wove the kiswa, the black embroidered covering of the Kaaba, renewed every year and carried to Mecca with the ceremonial camel-litter, the mahmal. Supplying the imperial capital with rice and beans was a further standing charge. These obligations were the price of the province's autonomy.
entries.note: Suraiya Faroqhi, Pilgrims and Sultans: The Hajj under the Ottomans (1994). Jane Hathaway, The Arab Lands under Ottoman Rule 1516–1800 (2008) pp.55–58, 152–58.

entries.label: The ulama as the notables of Cairo
entries.hint: The senior scholars of al-Azhar and the great mosques formed a self-perpetuating urban elite: they held tax farms and administered vast endowments, arbitrated between the rulers and the ruled, and spoke for the city in a crisis. In 1795, when Ibrahim and Murad Bey's new taxes provoked a shutdown of the markets, the shaykhs led the protest and extracted a written promise of relief. In the absence of any representative institution, the ulama were the nearest thing Egypt had to a civil society.
entries.note: Afaf Lutfi al-Sayyid Marsot, 'The Ulama of Cairo in the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries', in Keddie (ed.), Scholars, Saints, and Sufis (1972). Gabriel Baer, 'Popular Revolt in Ottoman Cairo', Der Islam 54 (1977). Al-Jabarti, passim.

entries.label: The guilds, the quarters and the market
entries.hint: The working city was organised in guilds — each trade a ta'ifa with its own shaykh, entry rules and internal court — and in residential quarters (harat), gated and closed at night under a headman and watchmen, sometimes with their own youth gangs. A market inspector (muhtasib) policed weights, prices and food quality. This dense fabric of small corporate bodies, rather than a municipal state, kept order in one of the world's largest cities.
entries.note: André Raymond, Artisans et commerçants au Caire au XVIIIe siècle (1973) and Cairo (2000). Gabriel Baer, Egyptian Guilds in Modern Times (1964).

entries.label: The waqf and the endowment economy
entries.hint: The religious endowment was everywhere. Rulers and merchants endowed mosques, drinking fountains (sabils), schools, hospitals and Sufi lodges, funding them from the rents of shops, houses, baths and farmland assigned in perpetuity. The 'family waqf' let an owner shelter property from the confiscations that regularly followed a bey's fall, drawing the income to his descendants as nominal administrators. A very large share of Cairo's real estate and much farmland was locked in waqf.
entries.note: Daniel Crecelius, 'The Waqf of Muhammad Bey Abu al-Dhahab', JESHO 34 (1991); Muhammad Afifi and the waqf-document scholarship. The registers of the Ministry of Awqaf, Cairo.

entries.label: The sharia courts and their registers
entries.hint: Justice ran through a hierarchy of sharia courts — the chief court of the Bab al-'Ali and dozens of neighbourhood tribunals — whose scribes kept bound registers (sijills) of every deed, contract, marriage, divorce, inheritance and dispute they handled. All four Sunni legal schools had their own judges. Christians and Jews, entitled to their own communal courts, frequently chose the Muslim court instead for property and family matters, trusting its record-keeping. The registers are the richest source for Ottoman Egyptian society.
entries.note: The Cairo court registers: studies by 'Abd al-Rahim 'Abd al-Rahman, Nelly Hanna, and Boğaç Ergene's methodological work. Nelly Hanna, Making Big Money in 1600: The Life and Times of Isma'il Abu Taqiyya (1998).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Al-Azhar as the centre of the Sunni world, the Sufi orders and the great mawlids, and the Coptic and Jewish communities

entries.label: al-Azhar, the centre of the Sunni world
entries.hint: Under the Ottomans al-Azhar became the pre-eminent seat of Sunni learning anywhere. Students came from West Africa, the Maghrib, Syria, the Hijaz, Anatolia, India and the Malay world, housed and fed in residence halls (riwaqs) organised by homeland and legal school. Instruction was free, given in circles around individual shaykhs who issued personal licences to teach; the curriculum ran from grammar and logic to law, hadith and Qurʾanic science. The office of shaykh al-Azhar, its head, took shape in this period.
entries.note: Bayard Dodge, Al-Azhar: A Millennium of Muslim Learning (1961); Jonathan Berkey, The Transmission of Knowledge in Medieval Cairo (1992) for the earlier system; Rudolph Peters, 'Reinhard Schulze's Quest for an Islamic Enlightenment', Die Welt des Islams 30 (1990) on the debate about the period.

entries.label: The Sufi orders and the great mawlids
entries.hint: Popular religion was organised by the Sufi brotherhoods — the Shadhiliyya, the Ahmadiyya of Sayyid al-Badawi, the Khalwatiyya, the Bakriyya whose head presided over the Cairo orders — with their lodges, litanies and public zikr. Their festivals were the largest gatherings in Egypt: the mawlid of al-Badawi at Tanta drew hundreds of thousands each autumn for a fair, a fair-ground and a religious carnival, and the Cairo mawlids of al-Husayn and al-Sayyida Zaynab filled whole quarters.
entries.note: F. de Jong, Turuq and Turuq-Linked Institutions in Nineteenth Century Egypt (1978). The Tanta mawlid: J.W. McPherson, The Moulids of Egypt (1941); Edward Lane, An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1836) for the mature form.

entries.label: The shrine city and the plague
entries.hint: Cairo was a landscape of holy tombs — the head-shrine of al-Husayn, the mosques of al-Sayyida Zaynab, al-Sayyida Nafisa and the imam al-Shafiʿi, and the inhabited 'cities of the dead' — and visiting them (ziyara) was everyday devotion. It became more so under the plague, which struck the city roughly every decade or two: the outbreak of 1791 is thought to have killed a fifth of Cairo. Debate on whether the faithful should flee an epidemic ran alongside processions with the Qurʾan and appeals to the saints.
entries.note: Michael Dols, The Black Death in the Middle East (1977) and the Ottoman-era continuation; Daniel Panzac, La peste dans l'Empire ottoman 1700–1850 (1985). Cairo's shrines: Caroline Williams, Islamic Monuments in Cairo (2008).

entries.label: The Coptic Church in the Ottoman centuries
entries.hint: The Coptic Church reached its lowest point in numbers and wealth in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, then revived in the eighteenth as the archon families poured money into it: churches rebuilt, the desert monasteries restored, and a flourishing of icon painting led by the Armenian immigrant Yuhanna al-Armani and his Coptic partner Ibrahim al-Nasikh. The patriarch went on sending the metropolitan bishop to Ethiopia. From 1741 a small Coptic Catholic community formed under Franciscan influence.
entries.note: Magdi Guirguis, An Armenian Artist in Ottoman Egypt: Yuhanna al-Armani and His Coptic Icons (2008); Febe Armanios, Coptic Christianity in Ottoman Egypt (2011).

entries.label: The Jewish community of Ottoman Egypt
entries.hint: Egypt's Jews — Rabbanite and Karaite, with a layer of Iberian exiles and, later, North African and Italian traders — were self-governing under their own leaders, though the old office of nagid, head of all Egyptian Jewry, lapsed around the Ottoman conquest. In practice the community was often represented by whichever Jewish financier held the post of chief banker (sarraf) to the treasury or the customs. Numbers and wealth declined over the period; the storeroom of the Ben Ezra synagogue kept filling with discarded documents.
entries.note: Jacob Landau, Jews in Nineteenth-Century Egypt (1969) for the later community; the Ottoman-era nagidate, Mark Cohen, Jewish Self-Government in Medieval Egypt (1980). The Geniza's long tail: S.D. Goitein.

entries.label: The stirrings of reform
entries.hint: Late in the period new currents moved. Pilgrims returning from Arabia carried word of the austere Wahhabi movement then rising in Najd, which rejected the whole culture of shrines and Sufi orders. Within al-Azhar, revivalist teachers pressed for a return to the founding texts. And a handful of scholars, the young Hasan al-'Attar chief among them, sought out the French savants of the Institut d'Égypte after 1798 to learn their sciences — the first Egyptian intellectuals to treat European knowledge as something to acquire rather than dismiss.
entries.note: Peter Gran, Islamic Roots of Capitalism: Egypt, 1760–1840 (1979) — the al-'Attar case. Al-Jabarti on the French Institut. The Wahhabi impact: Michael Cook and the Najdi sources.
